strengths: Originality: The resolution-dependent statistical formulation offers a useful perspective on image classification. Its main originality lies in analyzing deformation invariance and discretization, rather than in introducing a new classification architecture.

Significance: The crop–rescale–normalize classifier is simple and interpretable. The alignment analysis identifies useful relationships between resolution, support regularity, template separation, and the availability of labeled examples.

Presentation: The manuscript provides intuitive explanations of both classifiers and extensive mathematical derivations. The experiments include repeated runs and a multiple-template setting that probes an extension beyond the basic model.

Limitations and ethics: Sections 3 and 6 candidly discuss background noise, occlusion, multiple objects, and richer deformations. The exclusion of optimization analysis is explicit. No material research-ethics concern is apparent in the theoretical analysis and MNIST experiments.
weaknesses: Soundness— inconsistent deformation assumptions: Model (1) uses f(ξx−τ, ξ′y−τ′), whereas the visibility constraints in Assumptions 1 and 1′ correspond to the opposite shift convention. For example, ξ=ξ′=2 and τ=τ′=−1 satisfy the stated constraints but make every sampled pixel zero for templates supported in [1/4,3/4]². Support alignment and normalization are then undefined. The assumptions and proofs must be reconciled before the guarantees hold as stated.

Soundness—CNN approximation construction: Theorems 4.1–4.2 introduce Ξ without requiring |ξ|,|ξ′|≤Ξ almost surely, although the proof only searches scales in [−Ξ,Ξ]. Moreover, the filters constructed on page 35 normalize samples f_k(ξj/d,ξ′ℓ/d) over a grid containing zero and negative scales. These samples are identically zero whenever either scale is nonpositive, given the template support assumption, producing undefined filters. A corrected construction must explicitly handle translations, flips, and normalization. These gaps affect the approximation theorem underlying the CNN risk bound.

Soundness—existence of the estimator: Equation (17) assumes an exact empirical least-squares minimizer over networks with unrestricted weights and softmax outputs. On separable data, scaling the logits drives the loss toward zero, but finite logits cannot attain zero loss. Thus the stated argmin can be empty. An approximate minimizer or an appropriate parameter restriction is needed, with the corresponding change to the oracle analysis.

Soundness—optimality and rate claims: Theorem 3.5 establishes an unnormalized L2 distance for one fixed deformation; it does not lower-bound the normalized separation D minimized over all deformations in Theorem 3.4, nor establish the same Γ-regular support class. Consequently, it does not prove the advertised matching separation lower bound. Separately, substituting n proportional to d^(4+q) log^4(d) into (18) gives order d^(−q/2), not the stated d^(−q); the latter needs a stronger argument or a different sample-size scaling.

Significance and claim calibration: The introduction promises theoretical underpinning for data augmentation and extreme overparameterization, but augmentation remains conjectural, and the provided CNN consistency bound uses sample sizes exceeding the network parameter count up to logarithmic factors. The restricted template model can still be useful, but these broader explanatory claims exceed the established results.

Evaluation: All experiments fix d=28, so they do not test the central dependence on resolution or the proposed separation thresholds. The experimental CNNs use small filters and local pooling, substantially differing from the theoretical construction. Results with n=2–64 and median errors on 100 test examples illustrate the alignment method's advantage in this setting, but do not validate the CNN rate; uncertainty estimates are also absent.

Reproducibility and mathematical presentation: The manuscript provides no code link and omits template identifiers, deformation distributions/ranges, training loss, epochs, batch sizes, and seeds. These omissions prevent faithful reproduction of Figure 5. Mathematical proofreading is also needed: for example, page 13 thresholds a class probability at zero instead of one-half, and the final inequalities in the proof of Theorem 3.4 contain inconsistent constants.
